healthcare.domain_context: Scenarios happen inside hospitals, clinics, or care networks. Vary the decision-maker role across scenarios rather than defaulting to the same one -- charge nurses, attending physicians, case managers, pharmacy directors, OR/surgical scheduling directors, nursing supervisors, and department administrators all plausibly make binding calls in this domain. Vary the resource or stakes being decided too: bed or unit assignment, discharge destination and timing, operating-room block time, medication/formulary approval, staffing or shift coverage, referral or waitlist prioritization, equipment allocation, and on-call assignments are all fair game -- avoid defaulting to the same 'reassign a bed' or 'plan a discharge' shape every time. Vary the KIND of hidden lever as well, spreading it across categories: an uncharted clinical or lab finding, a logistical or equipment/scheduling constraint, an insurance or authorization rule, a family or caregiver circumstance, and a staffing or coverage conflict are all legitimate categories -- do not let every scenario's secret be 'a lab result nobody charted yet.' Private facts should read like ordinary clinical or logistical details a person in that role would plausibly know and might not think to volunteer unprompted. Avoid graphic medical detail; keep facts at the level of care-coordination information, not diagnosis descriptions. Commitments often take the form of care-plan conditions, follow-up appointments, staffing pledges, or facility/equipment requests rather than money. Scenarios in this domain commonly involve 3 to 5 agents -- as the agent count grows, add more distinct hidden-fact holders and decision-relevant departments (e.g. therapy, pharmacy, social work, nursing) rather than padding with agents who don't hold a decisive fact.

few_shot_examples.description: A charge nurse must assign the last available ICU bed between two patients being considered for transfer, with input from an attending physician and a patient-family liaison.

shared_context.S1: Two patients, in Bay 3 and Bay 7, are both being evaluated for the one open ICU bed.
shared_context.S2: Dana makes the final bed assignment.
shared_context.S3: Bay 3's patient had a procedure this morning that required one unit of transfused blood and is still on a post-op drip.
shared_context.S4: Bay 7's patient has been stable on the general floor for two days.
shared_context.S5: Before the assignment is finalized, Dana checks in with the attending and the family liaison for anything relevant.

PF1.text: Bay 7's patient's morning labs came back showing a temperature of 102.6F and a lactate of 2.9, meeting criteria for likely sepsis requiring ICU-level monitoring within the hour -- Dr. Okafor saw the numbers directly but the resident is still finishing the chart note.

PF2.text: Bay 7's patient also needs continuous pulse-oximetry monitoring for the next four hours, which the general floor cannot provide but the ICU can -- this was flagged in Dr. Okafor's exam note, which is still pending co-signature.

PF3.text: Bay 3's family mentioned to Priya in the hallway ten minutes ago that they would accept a step-down unit instead, if a step-down bed can be confirmed within two hours -- it hasn't been logged in the system yet.

acceptance_conditions: The ICU bed must go to Bay 7, because of the sepsis-risk labs.
Continuous pulse-oximetry monitoring must be ordered for Bay 7's patient.
A step-down bed request for Bay 3 must be logged as a commitment.
The step-down window must not exceed the two hours the family actually agreed to.
The sepsis finding must be explicitly cited as justification.

content_checks.C4: any(c['type'] == 'step_down_request' and c['target'] == 'Bay 3' for c in commitments)

provenance_checks.P1: 'PF1' in credited_facts and 'PF1' in justification_fact_ids and 'PF1' in revealed

decisive_facts.why: Bay 3 looks like the obvious pick on paper (fresh post-op, transfusion, still on a drip); without the sepsis labs, there is no reason to instead send the ICU bed to Bay 7.
Without knowing continuous pulse-ox monitoring is specifically required, a generic settlement might assign the ICU bed but never explicitly order the monitoring that justifies needing it.

Nothing public says Bay 3's family would accept a step-down bed, or on what timeline; without PF3, there's no reason to log that commitment, and no reason to cap the window at two hours rather than leaving it open-ended.

few_shot_examples.description: A surgical scheduling director must decide which of two surgeons gets an open Thursday operating-room block, with input from each surgeon's clinic coordinator and the sterile processing manager.

shared_context.S1: Thursday afternoon has one open 3-hour OR block that has not yet been assigned.
shared_context.S2: Marcus makes the final block assignment.
shared_context.S3: Both Dr. Reyes and Dr. Okonkwo have patients waiting for a similar elective procedure.
shared_context.S4: Before finalizing, Marcus checks in with both clinic coordinators and sterile processing for anything relevant.

PF1.text: Dr. Reyes's patient's biopsy came back showing a fast-growing tumor type; guidelines call for surgery within 10 days, and Thursday is the only slot before that window closes -- the results landed in Elena's inbox this morning and she hasn't updated the shared schedule yet.

PF2.text: Dr. Okonkwo already secured a backup Saturday-morning slot at the outpatient surgical center for this same patient earlier this week -- Tobias arranged it directly with the center and it isn't logged in the main scheduling system.

PF3.text: The specialized instrument tray Dr. Reyes's procedure requires takes 48 hours to sterilize and reprocess, so it must be requested by Tuesday morning to be ready for Thursday -- this lead time only shows up in sterile processing's own tracking log, not the scheduling software.

acceptance_conditions: The Thursday block must go to Dr. Reyes, given the 10-day surgical window on the biopsy finding.
The instrument tray must be requested by Tuesday, given the 48-hour sterilization lead time.
The existing backup Saturday slot for Dr. Okonkwo's patient must be explicitly confirmed in the plan.
The biopsy finding must be cited as justification for the block assignment.

content_checks.C4: any(c['type'] == 'instrument_request' and c['target'] == 'Sterile Processing' for c in commitments)

provenance_checks.P1: 'PF1' in credited_facts and 'PF1' in justification_fact_ids and 'PF1' in revealed

decisive_facts.why: Nothing public favors either surgeon; without the biopsy urgency, a scheduler has no forcing reason to give the block to Dr. Reyes over Dr. Okonkwo.
Without knowing a backup slot already exists, reassigning the block away from Dr. Okonkwo would look like an unaddressed access problem rather than a settled non-issue.

Without knowing the 48-hour sterilization lead time, there's no reason to request the tray specifically by Tuesday or log that request at all -- a generic plan would leave it until closer to Thursday.

few_shot_examples.description: A case manager must finalize a medically stable patient's discharge destination and care plan, with input from physical therapy, pharmacy, social work, and the primary nurse.

shared_context.S1: The patient is medically stable and being considered for discharge tomorrow.
shared_context.S2: Priya finalizes the discharge destination and care plan.
shared_context.S3: The patient has expressed a preference to go home if possible.
shared_context.S4: Before finalizing, Priya checks in with physical therapy, pharmacy, social work, and nursing for anything relevant.

PF1.text: The patient failed this morning's stair-climb and transfer assessment and cannot safely navigate stairs without supervised therapy for at least one to two weeks -- Jordan just finished writing it up and was planning to raise it at today's check-in, but it isn't in the chart yet.

PF2.text: The patient's new blood-thinner requires lab draws twice a week for the first month; home health in this area only offers weekly draws, but a rehab facility can do them onsite -- Amara confirmed this with the prescribing physician an hour ago and hasn't updated the discharge orders yet.

PF3.text: The patient's preferred rehab facility, Willowbrook, has no open bed until Monday, but Cedar Ridge, a comparable facility, has an opening tomorrow -- Dan got this update from Willowbrook by phone this morning and hasn't posted it to the shared placement board yet.

PF4.text: The patient's home caregiver, their daughter, texted the unit ten minutes ago that a family emergency will keep her out of town for the next eight days, so no one would be home to help.

acceptance_conditions: The patient must be discharged to rehab, not home, given the failed mobility assessment.
Cedar Ridge must be selected, since the preferred facility has no bed until Monday.
Lab monitoring must be set to onsite, since home health cannot meet the twice-weekly requirement.
A pharmacy order for the onsite monitoring must be logged.
A commitment to update the daughter on the plan must exist, given her unavailability.

content_checks.C4: any(c['type'] == 'inr_monitoring_order' and c['target'] == 'Pharmacy' for c in commitments)
content_checks.C5: any(c['type'] == 'family_communication' and c['target'] == 'Daughter' for c in commitments)

provenance_checks.P1: 'PF1' in credited_facts and 'PF1' in justification_fact_ids and 'PF1' in revealed

decisive_facts.why: The patient's own stated preference is to go home; without the failed mobility assessment, there is no reason to override that preference and choose rehab.
Without knowing home health can't meet the twice-weekly draw requirement, there is no reason to set monitoring to onsite or log a pharmacy order for it rather than defaulting to routine home health.
Without knowing Willowbrook has no bed until Monday, a generic plan would send the patient to the patient's actual preferred facility rather than Cedar Ridge.
Without knowing the daughter is unexpectedly unavailable, there is no reason to log a specific commitment to update her on the plan.

software_technology.domain_context: Scenarios happen inside a product/engineering org. Vary the decision-maker role rather than defaulting to the same one -- engineering managers, tech leads, CTOs, product directors, platform/infra leads, and security engineering managers all plausibly make binding calls here. Vary the decision type too: sprint/release scope, incident postmortems, architecture or vendor selection, migration or cutover go/no-go calls, on-call staffing and pager rotations, technical-debt paydown prioritization, security patch rollout timing, feature-flag rollout decisions, and infra capacity/cost calls are all fair game -- avoid defaulting to the same 'ship or cut a feature' shape every time. Vary the KIND of hidden lever as well: an undocumented tech-debt shortcut, a flaky test nobody escalated, a customer SLA or contract clause, an on-call burnout signal, a security finding not yet ticketed, a cost/billing anomaly, a dependency vulnerability, a performance regression, a compliance/audit deadline, or a conflicting deploy window with another team -- do not let every scenario's secret be 'an undiscovered bug.' Private facts should read like ordinary engineering reality someone would plausibly know from their own work and might not think to proactively broadcast -- always give a concrete, mundane reason the information hasn't reached the decision-maker yet (found it during a different task, confirmed it minutes ago, hasn't filed the ticket/finding yet), never silence for no reason. Commitments often take the form of scope cuts, follow-up tickets, staffing changes, or customer communications rather than money. Scenarios in this domain commonly involve 3 to 5 agents -- as the count grows, add more distinct hidden-fact holders and decision-relevant functions (e.g. security, infra, support, QA) rather than padding with agents who don't hold a decisive fact.

few_shot_examples.description: An engineering manager must decide whether to ship a feature in the current release or cut it, with input from a senior developer and the QA lead.

shared_context.S1: The release is scheduled to ship Friday.
shared_context.S2: Sam makes the final call on what ships.
shared_context.S3: The new export feature has passed all planned functional test cases and load-tested cleanly up to 5,000 rows in yesterday's QA run.
shared_context.S4: Before the release is finalized, Sam asks the team for any last concerns.

PF1.text: While profiling an unrelated ticket last night, Priya found that the export feature's data pipeline silently drops rows above 10,000 records -- well past what yesterday's QA run tested -- but she hasn't filed a bug for it yet.

PF2.text: There's also no automated alert configured for row-count anomalies on this pipeline, so a silent drop like this wouldn't be caught until a customer complained; Priya noticed this while investigating the bug but hasn't raised it in the release channel.

PF3.text: Jordan confirmed with the QA rotation this morning that a fix for the row-limit issue could be tested and verified by Thursday if flagged today, but hasn't posted that in the release channel yet.

acceptance_conditions: The row-limit fix must be scheduled before Friday.
The feature must still ship, since a same-week fix is possible.
The fix must be due by Thursday specifically.
A monitoring alert for row-count anomalies must be added.
The silent data-loss risk must be cited as justification for the fix.

decisive_facts.why: The feature looks release-ready from passing tests alone; without PF1, there's no reason to schedule a row-limit fix at all.
Without knowing there's no alerting on row-count anomalies, a generic fix-and-ship plan wouldn't think to add monitoring for the underlying class of bug.
Without knowing a fix is achievable specifically by Thursday, the safe generic response is to delay the whole feature rather than ship on schedule with a Thursday-dated fix.

few_shot_examples.description: A team lead must decide the remediation plan after a production outage, with input from an on-call SRE, a product manager, and a security engineer.

shared_context.S1: Yesterday's outage lasted 40 minutes and affected the billing API.
shared_context.S2: Alex writes the final remediation plan.
shared_context.S3: The immediate cause was a bad config push.
shared_context.S4: Alex asks the team for anything the postmortem should include.

PF1.text: The config push succeeded because the staging validation step has been silently disabled for three weeks; Noor traced this to the root cause overnight while investigating the incident but hasn't filed the finding yet.

PF2.text: The affected enterprise customer's contract includes a service-credit penalty triggered by any outage over 30 minutes unless a root-cause fix is committed within 5 business days; Ben confirmed this with legal an hour ago but hasn't updated the incident channel yet.

PF3.text: The same disabled validation step also means a scheduled security patch for a known vulnerability in the billing API never actually deployed last week; Priya found this while auditing the incident this morning but hasn't opened a ticket yet.

acceptance_conditions: Staging validation must be restored.
A committed fix deadline of at most 5, at least 1, business days must exist.
The disabled validation step must be cited as the real root cause.
The pending security patch must be deployed.
A security-patch commitment must be logged.

decisive_facts.why: The bad config push looks like the root cause on its own; without PF1, there's no reason to touch staging validation at all.
Without the contract penalty clause, there's no forcing reason to commit to a specific 1-5 business day fix instead of an open-ended placeholder.
Without knowing the security patch never deployed, the remediation plan would only address the outage and miss the still-open vulnerability entirely.

few_shot_examples.description: A CTO must decide whether to proceed with tonight's planned production database migration and finalize the window, rollback, and customer-communication plan, with input from a senior backend engineer, the database/infrastructure lead, the customer support lead, and a security engineer.

shared_context.S1: Tonight's 11 PM-3 AM maintenance window is reserved for the planned production database migration.
shared_context.S2: Morgan makes the final go/no-go call for the migration.
shared_context.S3: The migration has passed all planned tests in the staging environment.
shared_context.S4: Before finalizing, Morgan checks with backend engineering, database/infra, customer support, and security for anything relevant.

PF1.text: While reviewing the migration script this afternoon, Devon found that the rollback script doesn't correctly restore a specific index used by billing queries, meaning a rollback after a certain point would leave billing queries degraded for hours; he hasn't filed anything on this yet.

PF2.text: Sasha confirmed this morning that the actual production data volume is 40% larger than staging, meaning the migration will take approximately 5.5 hours rather than the runbook's estimated 3 -- pushing the finish to around 4:30 AM -- but this isn't updated in the maintenance ticket yet.

PF3.text: Elena found while reviewing the account list this morning that one major enterprise customer's contract requires 48 hours' advance notice for any maintenance affecting their region, and that customer hasn't been notified; she hasn't raised this yet.

PF4.text: Kai confirmed this week that postponing tonight's migration would delay a mandatory patch for a critical vulnerability that must be applied by Friday, since the patch depends on the new schema; he flagged this internally but hasn't escalated it formally.

acceptance_conditions: The migration must proceed tonight, since postponing risks missing Friday's mandatory patch deadline.
The window must be extended to 4:30 AM to reflect the true migration duration.
The rollback script must be fixed before the migration starts.
The contractually-protected customer's shard must be deferred to a properly-noticed date.
A customer-notification commitment naming that customer must exist.

decisive_facts.why: Without knowing the rollback script is broken, there is no reason to require it be fixed before the migration starts.
Without the real 5.5-hour duration, a generic plan would keep the runbook's 3-hour estimate and set the end time around 2 AM instead of 4:30 AM.
Without knowing about the 48-hour-notice customer, there is no reason to carve out and defer that specific shard or make a targeted notification commitment.

Without knowing postponing risks missing Friday's mandatory patch deadline, the generic cautious choice given three other open risks (PF1-PF3) would be to postpone the whole migration rather than proceed.

defense.domain_context: Scenarios happen inside a military or defense-logistics unit. Keep content at the level of routine operational logistics and planning -- never depict combat violence, casualties, or weapons use; the tension is entirely about incomplete information (intel timing, fuel/maintenance status, competing mission priorities, personnel readiness), not violence. Vary the decision-maker role rather than defaulting to the same one -- convoy commanders, battalion XOs, company commanders, S-4 logistics officers, S-3 operations officers, and FOB commanders all plausibly make binding calls here. Vary the decision type too: route selection, equipment or radio allocation, fuel/POL distribution, maintenance prioritization, training or rotation scheduling, personnel assignment, and base facility or access planning are all fair game -- avoid defaulting to the same 'choose between two options' shape every time. Vary the KIND of hidden lever as well: intel timing, equipment/maintenance status, a competing mission priority, a personnel readiness or qualification gap, a supply-chain or logistics timing constraint, a terrain/weather factor, or a higher-headquarters directive not yet disseminated -- do not let every scenario's secret be 'an intel report.' Private facts should read like ordinary staff-officer knowledge someone would plausibly have from their own lane of work -- always give a concrete, mundane reason the information hasn't reached the decision-maker yet (confirmed this morning, still being verified, not yet on the briefing slide, not yet posted to the order), never silence for no reason. Commitments often take the form of route changes, resupply requests, or reassignment orders rather than money. Scenarios in this domain commonly involve 3 to 5 agents -- as the count grows, add more distinct hidden-fact holders and staff functions (e.g. intel, logistics, signal, aviation, medical) rather than padding with agents who don't hold a decisive fact.

few_shot_examples.description: A convoy commander must choose between two supply routes and set the departure timing, with input from an intelligence officer and a logistics officer.

shared_context.S1: Route Alpha is 20 minutes shorter than Route Bravo.
shared_context.S2: Capt. Reyes gives the final routing order.
shared_context.S3: The convoy must reach the forward base before nightfall, and Route Alpha has been the lower-traffic option for most of this month.
shared_context.S4: Before departure, Capt. Reyes asks the intel and logistics officers for anything relevant.

PF1.text: An unconfirmed field report from an hour ago flags increased irregular checkpoint activity specifically along Route Alpha; Lt. Chen is still verifying the source and hasn't included it in this morning's briefing yet.

PF2.text: There's also a confirmed 45-minute window today, 10:00 to 10:45, when a partner-unit patrol will be clearing that same stretch of Route Alpha, which would add further risk if the convoy overlapped with it; Lt. Chen hasn't cross-checked this against the convoy's planned departure time yet.

PF3.text: Route Bravo's bridge crossing has a load restriction requiring the convoy to split into two smaller groups, adding roughly 25 minutes; Sgt. Watts confirmed this with the bridge engineers this morning, but the updated restriction hasn't been posted to the movement order yet.

acceptance_conditions: Route Bravo must be selected, given the checkpoint-activity report on Alpha.
Departure must be set to 11:00 to clear the partner-unit patrol window.
The convoy split required by Bravo's bridge restriction must be planned for.
The extra transit time from splitting must be estimated at 20-40 minutes.
The checkpoint-activity report must be cited as justification.

decisive_facts.why: Route Alpha is the faster, historically-lower-traffic default; without PF1, there is no reason to divert to Bravo.
Without knowing about the 10:00-10:45 overlap window, a generic plan would not push departure to specifically 11:00.
Without knowing Bravo's bridge forces a convoy split adding roughly 25 minutes, the plan would neither split the convoy, estimate the time cost, nor log a split plan.

few_shot_examples.description: A battalion executive officer must allocate a limited shipment of new radios between two company commanders and finalize when the radios will actually be operational, with input from both company commanders and the signal officer.

shared_context.S1: Only 12 new radios arrived, enough to fully equip one company but not both.
shared_context.S2: Maj. Kim makes the final allocation.
shared_context.S3: Both companies are currently within radio range of battalion headquarters.
shared_context.S4: The signal shop can begin programming radios as soon as they're allocated, starting at 0800 today.
shared_context.S5: Before deciding, Maj. Kim asks both commanders and the signal officer for anything relevant to the allocation.

PF1.text: Company A's current radios have a confirmed intermittent failure rate that already caused two missed check-ins this week; Capt. Diallo confirmed this with the commo section this week but hasn't submitted an equipment-readiness report yet.

PF2.text: Company B is scheduled to begin an extended patrol rotation with degraded communications coverage starting in three days; Capt. Ibrahim received the rotation order yesterday but hasn't briefed battalion staff on the timeline yet.

PF3.text: The new radios require encryption-key loading and frequency programming that takes exactly 6 hours per full company set, and the shop can only process one company's set before end of day; Lt. Osei learned this from the shop supervisor this morning but hasn't flagged the timeline to battalion yet.

acceptance_conditions: The radios must go to Company A, given its confirmed equipment failures.
A repair request for Company B's existing radios must be logged, within 1-3 days.
The radios must be recorded as operational by 1400, given the 6-hour programming time starting at 0800.
The equipment-failure report must be cited as justification.

content_checks.C3: any(c['type'] == 'equipment_repair' and c['target'] == 'Company B' for c in commitments)

decisive_facts.why: Without the confirmed failure report, there is no basis to prefer Company A over a generic even split or seniority-based call.
Without knowing Company B's rotation starts in three days, there is no urgency to request a repair at all, let alone within that specific window.
Without knowing programming takes 6 hours starting at 0800, a generic plan would not set a specific 1400 operational time.

few_shot_examples.description: A forward operating base commander must allocate this week's constrained fuel delivery among ground operations, motor pool maintenance, aviation, and MEDEVAC standby, with input from the S-4 logistics officer, the motor pool maintenance chief, the aviation liaison, and the MEDEVAC coordinator.

shared_context.S1: This week's fuel delivery is 4,000 gallons.
shared_context.S2: Col. Whitfield makes the final fuel allocation and resupply plan.
shared_context.S3: Standard weekly requests are 2,000 gallons for ground operations, 1,500 for motor pool, and a 1,000-gallon standing reserve floor for aviation.
shared_context.S4: Before finalizing, Col. Whitfield holds the routine weekly logistics huddle with S-4, motor pool, aviation, and MEDEVAC for any updates to their standard requests.

PF1.text: Maj. Bishop confirmed this morning that 2nd Platoon's patrol schedule was extended by three additional days this week, requiring exactly 800 gallons above the standard ground request; the updated patrol order hasn't been reflected in the fuel request yet.

PF2.text: SFC Nunez found during this week's vehicle inspection that two support vehicles need extended idle-time for battery reconditioning, consuming exactly 300 gallons beyond the standard motor-pool request; the finding is in his inspection log but hasn't been submitted to logistics yet.

PF3.text: Capt. Delgado confirmed with the flight surgeon's office this morning that aviation's fuel reserve cannot go below 1,200 gallons at any point this week without grounding the standby MEDEVAC helicopter -- 200 gallons above the standard floor -- but hasn't updated the standing order yet.

PF4.text: Lt. Park confirmed that Thursday's scheduled route-clearance operation requires MEDEVAC to hold an additional 150-gallon reserve strictly for the helicopter's post-mission return leg, on top of aviation's standing floor; this is in the operation's support annex but hasn't been cross-referenced with the fuel plan yet.

acceptance_conditions: Ground operations must receive exactly 800 extra gallons for the extended patrol.
Motor pool must receive exactly 300 extra gallons for battery reconditioning.
Aviation's reserve floor must be raised to exactly 1,200 gallons.
MEDEVAC's Thursday reserve must be set to exactly 150 gallons.
A commitment formally updating the fuel request must exist.

decisive_facts.why: Without knowing about the patrol extension, there is no reason to add 800 gallons above the standard ground request.
Without knowing about the battery reconditioning need, there is no reason to add 300 gallons above the standard motor-pool request.
Without knowing the MEDEVAC-linked floor rose to 1,200, the reserve would stay at the standard 1,000-gallon floor, risking grounding the standby helicopter.
Without knowing about Thursday's operation-specific reserve requirement, there is no reason to set aside the additional 150 gallons.

finance.domain_context: Scenarios happen inside a bank, fund, or corporate finance team. Vary the decision-maker role rather than defaulting to the same one -- credit officers, portfolio managers, finance directors, treasury directors, underwriting managers, and risk committee chairs all plausibly make binding calls here. Vary the decision type too: loan approval, portfolio rebalancing, budget sign-off, covenant waivers, credit line renewals, capital expenditure approval, hedging decisions, and cash/liquidity allocation are all fair game -- avoid defaulting to the same 'approve or decline' shape every time. Vary the KIND of hidden lever as well: an unlogged risk flag, a compliance or regulatory constraint, a client relationship detail, a liquidity note, a covenant breach not yet reported, a related-party disclosure, a pending policy change, an internal audit finding, or a counterparty concentration issue -- do not let every scenario's secret be 'a credit score dropped.' Private facts should read like ordinary desk-level information someone would plausibly have from their own coverage area -- always give a concrete, mundane reason the information hasn't reached the decision-maker yet (confirmed this morning, just received in a memo, found while reviewing a file this week, not yet circulated or logged), never silence for no reason. Commitments often take the form of covenants, monitoring requirements, or conditional approvals rather than a simple yes/no. Scenarios in this domain commonly involve 3 to 5 agents -- as the count grows, add more distinct hidden-fact holders and desk functions (e.g. risk, compliance, trading, client coverage) rather than padding with agents who don't hold a decisive fact.

few_shot_examples.description: A credit officer must decide whether to approve a small-business loan and its conditions, with input from a risk analyst and a relationship manager.

shared_context.S1: The applicant is requesting a $150,000 working-capital loan.
shared_context.S2: Farah makes the final approval decision.
shared_context.S3: The applicant's submitted financials show two years of steady revenue.
shared_context.S4: Before deciding, Farah asks the risk analyst and relationship manager for anything relevant.

PF1.text: A recent credit-bureau pull, not yet in the file, shows the applicant's personal credit score dropped sharply last month due to a separate missed payment.

PF2.text: Because of the credit dip, standard desk practice also calls for a quarterly financial-reporting covenant on any approval; Colin noted this in his draft risk memo but hasn't attached it to the file yet.

PF3.text: The applicant has agreed, if asked, to pledge a delivery vehicle worth $20,000 as additional collateral, which would cover the loan gap.

acceptance_conditions: Additional collateral of at least $20,000, and no more than $25,000, must be required.
The loan must still be approved, since the collateral gap is coverable.
A quarterly reporting covenant must be attached given standard practice for this risk profile.
The credit-score drop must be cited as justification for requiring collateral.

decisive_facts.why: The file looks clean on steady revenue alone; without PF1, there is no reason to require any collateral at all, so a generic settlement would leave collateral_value_pledged_usd at 0, failing both the floor and the reason for a ceiling.
Without knowing standard practice calls for a reporting covenant at this risk profile, a generic settlement would approve the loan with collateral but skip the covenant entirely.
Without knowing collateral is actually available, the safe generic response to a credit-score drop is to decline the loan outright rather than approve it conditionally.

few_shot_examples.description: A portfolio manager must decide whether to rebalance a client fund out of a large equity position and finalize the execution and client-notification plan, with input from a compliance officer, a trader, and the client relationship manager.

shared_context.S1: The fund currently holds 18% of its assets in a single equity position.
shared_context.S2: Wei makes the final rebalancing decision.
shared_context.S3: The position has performed well over the past year.
shared_context.S4: Before deciding, Wei asks compliance, the trading desk, and client relations for anything relevant.

PF1.text: A new internal concentration limit caps any single position at 15% of fund assets; Sofia just received this in this morning's compliance memo but hasn't circulated it to portfolio managers yet.

PF2.text: Selling down the position in a single trade would move the market price; Marco confirmed with the desk's liquidity model this morning that a staged sell-down over three days avoids meaningful slippage.

PF3.text: The client's investment management agreement requires 5 business days' advance notice before any position exceeding 10% of the fund is reduced by more than a third; Priya found this clause while reviewing the agreement this week but hasn't flagged it to the desk yet.

acceptance_conditions: The position must be rebalanced down to comply with the new 15% limit.
The sell-down must be staged over 3-7 days rather than executed in a single trade.
The client must be given at least 5 business days' notice before the reduction.
The new concentration limit must be cited as justification.

decisive_facts.why: The position looks fine on strong past performance alone; without PF1, there's no compliance reason to rebalance at all.
Without knowing about slippage risk and the specific 3-day staging window, a generic rebalancing decision would not specify staging the trade at all, let alone over that timeframe.
Without knowing about the 5-day notice clause in the client's agreement, a generic plan would execute the trade without any client notice period.

few_shot_examples.description: A treasury director must decide whether to execute a foreign-currency hedge for a large customer receivable and finalize the counterparty split, tenor, and disclosure plan, with input from a credit risk analyst, a corporate treasury analyst, a sales relationship manager, and a compliance officer.

shared_context.S1: The customer receivable is $2,000,000, denominated in euros, due in 90 days.
shared_context.S2: Renata makes the final hedge decision.
shared_context.S3: The company's standard hedge ratio for receivables like this is 100% of notional, typically placed with Meridian Bank for its favorable rate.
shared_context.S4: Before finalizing, Renata checks with credit risk, treasury, sales, and compliance for anything relevant.

PF1.text: Owen flagged this morning that Meridian Bank has a credit rating downgrade under review, and internal policy caps hedge notional with any counterparty under review at $1,000,000; he hasn't logged this in the counterparty risk system yet.

PF2.text: Ines confirmed with the customer's AP team this morning that payment will likely arrive 15 days early, changing the effective hedge tenor from 90 to 75 days; this hasn't been updated in the treasury system yet.

PF3.text: The customer specifically asked, in a call last week, that the hedge counterparty not be Cascade Bank due to a prior billing dispute; Marcus has this in his call notes but hasn't flagged it to treasury yet.

PF4.text: Dana confirmed this week that hedges tied to receivables from this customer's jurisdiction require a regulatory disclosure filed within 2 business days of execution, under a rule that took effect last month; she flagged this internally but hasn't updated the compliance checklist yet.

acceptance_conditions: Notional placed with Meridian Bank must be between $500,000 and $1,000,000, given the rating review.
The hedge tenor must be set to 75 days, given the early-payment update.
Cascade Bank must be excluded as a counterparty, given the customer's request.
A regulatory disclosure must be filed within 1-2 business days of execution.

decisive_facts.why: The standard practice is 100% notional with Meridian Bank at its favorable rate; without PF1, there is no reason to cap notional there instead of placing the full $2,000,000.
Without knowing about the early payment, a generic hedge would use the standard 90-day tenor instead of 75.
Without knowing about the customer's objection, there is no reason to exclude Cascade Bank as a counterparty option.
Without knowing about the new disclosure rule, a generic hedge execution would not file any regulatory disclosure at all.

education.domain_context: Scenarios happen inside a school or college. Vary the decision-maker role rather than defaulting to the same one -- principals, department heads, counselors, special education coordinators, assistant principals, and curriculum directors all plausibly make binding calls here. Vary the decision type too: student placement, discipline and behavior plans, field-trip or activity logistics, IEP/504 accommodation decisions, resource or budget requests, staffing/substitute coverage, facility or room scheduling, and testing-accommodation approval are all fair game -- avoid defaulting to the same 'choose between two options' shape every time. Vary the KIND of hidden lever as well: an IEP or 504 requirement, a behavioral-fit note from a teacher, a budget cap from the office, a safety or medical concern, a scheduling conflict, a compliance or legal deadline, a family circumstance, or a staffing certification gap -- do not let every scenario's secret be 'a hidden accessibility need.' Private facts should read like ordinary school's or college's administration knowledge someone would plausibly have from their own role -- a teacher's own classroom observation or a counselor's own file review needs no extra explanation, but a fact that required active checking (calling a vendor, reviewing a compliance calendar, confirming with a family) should say so briefly, and always give a concrete reason it hasn't reached the decision-maker yet if it easily could have. Commitments often take the form of accommodations, staffing changes, or budget conditions. Scenarios in this domain commonly involve 3 to 5 agents -- as the count grows, add more distinct hidden-fact holders and school functions (e.g. teaching, counseling, health, family liaison, specialist services) rather than padding with agents who don't hold a decisive fact.

few_shot_examples.description: A principal must decide which class a transferring student joins and finalize the accommodation plan, with input from a teacher and a school counselor.

shared_context.S1: A transferring student needs to be placed in one of two 5th-grade classes.
shared_context.S2: Ms. Alvarez makes the final placement decision.
shared_context.S3: Mr. Doyle's class has a strong track record integrating students with support needs, based on last year's parent feedback.
shared_context.S4: Before deciding, Ms. Alvarez asks the teacher and counselor for anything relevant.

PF1.text: Mr. Doyle's class already has two students with significant behavioral support needs, and adding a third would exceed what one aide can manage; he raised this at this week's team meeting but it hasn't been noted in the placement tracker yet.

PF2.text: The transferring student's file includes an active IEP requiring a classroom aide be present at all times.

PF3.text: The IEP also specifies the aide must be confirmed and in place within 5 school days of enrollment, per the district's special-education compliance calendar; Ms. Freeman found this while reviewing the timeline this week but hasn't flagged the deadline to the office yet.

acceptance_conditions: The student must be placed in the other class, given Mr. Doyle's aide capacity.
Aide coverage must be full-day, given the IEP requirement.
A formal aide-assignment commitment must be logged.
A record confirming IEP compliance must be logged.
The aide must be confirmed within 1-5 school days, per the compliance timeline.

decisive_facts.why: Doyle's class looks like the stronger placement given its track record; without PF1, there is no reason to place the student elsewhere.
Without the IEP requirement, there is no reason to assign any aide, let alone full-day coverage or a formal compliance log.
Without knowing about the 5-day compliance deadline, a generic aide-assignment plan would not set a specific confirmation timeline.

few_shot_examples.description: A department head must approve the vendor, budget, and medical-staffing plan for an upcoming field trip, with input from the lead teacher, the school's business office liaison, and the school nurse.

shared_context.S1: Two bus vendors have submitted quotes for the trip.
shared_context.S2: Mr. Suarez gives final approval on vendor, budget, and staffing.
shared_context.S3: Vendor A's quote is $200 cheaper than Vendor B's.
shared_context.S4: Before approving, Mr. Suarez asks the lead teacher, business office, and school nurse for anything relevant.

PF1.text: Vendor A's buses lack the wheelchair lift needed for a student on this trip; Ms. Whitfield called the vendor's dispatcher this week to confirm accessibility features and learned this, but hasn't updated the trip planning sheet yet.

PF2.text: The trip's total budget, including Vendor B's higher quote, is already approved and does not need additional sign-off.

PF3.text: One student on the trip carries an EpiPen for a severe allergy, and district policy requires a staff member trained in epinephrine administration to ride on the same bus; Nurse Patel confirmed this with the student's health plan this week but hasn't flagged it to the trip organizers yet.

acceptance_conditions: Vendor B must be selected, given Vendor A's lack of accessibility.
No additional budget approval should be flagged as needed.
Wheelchair-lift availability must be explicitly confirmed.
A trained staff member must be assigned to the student's bus, given the EpiPen need.
The accessibility gap must be cited as justification.

decisive_facts.why: Vendor A looks like the obvious cheaper pick; without PF1, there is no reason to pay more for Vendor B or confirm a wheelchair lift.
Without knowing the higher quote is already covered, a cautious generic response would flag needing more budget approval.
Without knowing about the EpiPen requirement, there is no reason to assign a trained staff member to that specific bus.

few_shot_examples.description: A special education coordinator must finalize a student's annual IEP placement and services plan, with input from the general education teacher, the school psychologist, the speech-language pathologist, and the parent liaison.

shared_context.S1: The student's annual IEP review is scheduled for this week.
shared_context.S2: Ms. Chen finalizes the placement and services plan.
shared_context.S3: The student has been performing at grade level in general education classes with periodic support.
shared_context.S4: The current IEP specifies 30 minutes of daily one-on-one support and weekly speech therapy.
shared_context.S5: Before finalizing, Ms. Chen asks the teacher, psychologist, speech-language pathologist, and parent liaison for anything relevant.

PF1.text: Mr. Alvarez has noticed the student needs about 15 minutes more one-on-one redirection during transitions than the current plan accounts for; he mentioned this informally to a colleague but hasn't documented it in the IEP progress notes yet.

PF2.text: Dr. Osei's recent testing shows the student's processing speed score dropped into a range that newly qualifies for extended time on assessments; the report is finalized but hasn't been entered into the IEP system yet.

PF3.text: Ms. Reyes recommends increasing speech therapy from once to twice weekly, based on this semester's slower-than-expected progress data; she finalized this recommendation this week but hasn't submitted the service-minutes change yet.

PF4.text: The family has a work schedule conflict that makes the currently proposed Tuesday/Thursday after-school therapy slot impossible, but confirmed this week that Monday/Wednesday would work; Mr. Kim hasn't updated the scheduling system yet.

acceptance_conditions: Daily one-on-one support must increase to 45 minutes.
Extended time on assessments must be added as an accommodation.
Speech therapy must increase to twice weekly.
The therapy schedule must move to Monday/Wednesday.
A formal IEP documentation commitment must exist.

decisive_facts.why: Without knowing about the extra 15 minutes of transition support needed, the plan would keep the current 30-minute baseline.
Without the new processing-speed finding, there is no basis to add extended time as an accommodation.
Without the therapist's updated recommendation, the plan would keep speech therapy at once weekly.
Without knowing about the family's schedule conflict and the confirmed alternative, the plan would keep the unworkable Tuesday/Thursday slot.

entertainment.domain_context: Scenarios happen inside a production, festival, or studio: lineup scheduling, reshoot budgets, casting or booking calls. Decision-makers are typically producers, programmers, or showrunners. Private facts should read like ordinary industry logistics: a rider clause, an equipment constraint, a footage-quality note, an insurance detail. Commitments often take the form of schedule changes, budget line items, or contract riders.

few_shot_examples.description: A festival programmer must decide the closing set time, with input from the stage manager and an artist liaison.

shared_context.S1: Two acts, Nova and Ember, are both being considered for the closing headline slot.
shared_context.S2: Robin makes the final scheduling call.
shared_context.S3: Nova has the larger existing local fanbase.
shared_context.S4: Before finalizing, Robin asks the stage manager and artist liaison for anything relevant.

PF1.text: Nova's stage setup requires 45 minutes of changeover time that would push the venue past its city noise curfew.

PF2.text: Ember's contract rider includes a clause guaranteeing the closing slot if requested, which Ember's team has verbally confirmed they will invoke.

acceptance_conditions: Ember must close, honoring the rider clause.
The curfew risk from Nova's changeover must be addressed by scheduling Nova earlier, with at least 45 minutes of buffer before curfew.
The rider clause must be cited as justification.

content_checks.C3: any(c['type'] == 'schedule_change' and c['target'] == 'Nova' for c in commitments)

decisive_facts.why: Without knowing about the 45-minute changeover/curfew conflict, there is no reason to move Nova's set earlier at all, let alone by that specific margin.
Nova's bigger fanbase makes it the obvious closing pick; without the rider clause, there's no reason to give the slot to Ember instead.

few_shot_examples.description: A producer must decide whether to approve a reshoot for a key scene, with input from the director and the production accountant.

shared_context.S1: The scene in question was shot on location last week.
shared_context.S2: Elaine makes the final call on approving any reshoot.
shared_context.S3: A reshoot would cost roughly $40,000 in crew and location fees.
shared_context.S4: Before deciding, Elaine asks the director and accountant for anything relevant.

PF1.text: The audio track for the scene has an unfixable wind-noise problem that makes the dialogue unusable in post.

PF2.text: The production's insurance policy covers up to $50,000 for reshoots caused by an unusable original take, if filed within two weeks of the original shoot.

acceptance_conditions: The reshoot must be approved, given the unusable audio.
An insurance claim must be filed to cover the cost, within the required two-week window.
The unusable-audio finding must be cited as justification.

decisive_facts.why: Without knowing the audio is genuinely unusable, a cost-conscious producer would decline the $40,000 reshoot.
Without knowing insurance would cover it, and only within two weeks, there is no reason to file a claim at all, let alone within that specific deadline.

legal.domain_context: Scenarios happen inside a law firm or in-house legal team. Vary the decision-maker role rather than defaulting to the same one -- lead attorneys, general counsel, deputy general counsel, litigation directors, and chief legal officers all plausibly make binding calls here. Vary the decision type too: settlement authority, contract renewal, litigation strategy, IP licensing, employment dispute resolution, M&A due diligence go/no-go, and regulatory filing decisions are all fair game -- avoid defaulting to the same 'settle or renew' shape every time. Vary the KIND of hidden lever as well: a precedent not yet briefed, a client's non-monetary priority, an audit finding, a pricing benchmark, a privilege/conflict-of-interest issue, a filing or statute-of-limitations deadline, a discovery finding, or an insurance-coverage detail -- do not let every scenario's secret be 'a case-law finding.' Private facts should read like ordinary case-file or business detail someone would plausibly have from their own coverage area -- an attorney's own legal research or a liaison's own conversation with the client needs no extra explanation, but a fact that required active checking (reviewing a document set, confirming with another department) should say so briefly, and always give a concrete reason it hasn't reached the decision-maker yet if it easily could have. Commitments often take the form of settlement terms, contract clauses, or compliance actions rather than bare dollar figures alone. Scenarios in this domain commonly involve 3 to 5 agents -- as the count grows, add more distinct hidden-fact holders and legal/business functions (e.g. compliance, tax, HR, IP) rather than padding with agents who don't hold a decisive fact.

few_shot_examples.description: A lead attorney must set the firm's settlement offer terms in a contract dispute, with input from a junior associate and the client liaison.

shared_context.S1: The dispute involves a claimed $80,000 in damages.
shared_context.S2: Ms. Patel sets the final settlement offer.
shared_context.S3: The opposing party's initial counteroffer was $65,000, and they've signaled general openness to settling out of court.
shared_context.S4: Before finalizing the offer, Ms. Patel asks the associate and client liaison for anything relevant.

PF1.text: A recent appellate ruling in a near-identical case caps recoverable damages at $50,000 in this jurisdiction; Jon found this while researching a related motion this week but hasn't circulated it in a memo yet.

PF2.text: The same ruling requires any settlement relying on the cap to explicitly cite the case by name in the agreement to preserve its legal protection; Jon noted this in his research but hasn't flagged it as a drafting requirement yet.

PF3.text: The client mentioned directly to Renata during this week's check-in call that a public non-disparagement clause matters more to them than the exact settlement amount.

acceptance_conditions: The offer amount must be set at exactly the $50,000 appellate cap.
A non-disparagement clause must be included, with public scope specifically.
The settlement agreement must cite the appellate case by name to preserve the cap.
The appellate ruling must be cited as justification for the offer amount.

decisive_facts.why: With the opposing party's $65,000 counteroffer as the anchor, a generic negotiation would land somewhere between $65,000 and $80,000; without PF1, there is no reason to offer the much lower $50,000 cap.
Without knowing the citation requirement, a generic settlement at the correct amount would still fail to preserve the cap's legal protection.
Without knowing the client's real priority is public non-disparagement specifically, a generic settlement focused only on the dollar amount would omit the clause or include a private-only version.

few_shot_examples.description: A general counsel must decide whether to renew a vendor contract and finalize the compliance and pricing conditions, with input from a compliance counsel, a procurement lead, and a data privacy officer.

shared_context.S1: The vendor's current contract expires in two weeks.
shared_context.S2: Mr. Osei decides whether to renew.
shared_context.S3: The vendor has met all delivery deadlines this year.
shared_context.S4: Before deciding, Mr. Osei asks compliance, procurement, and data privacy for anything relevant.

PF1.text: An internal audit, not yet finalized, found the vendor's data-handling practices fall short of the required certification standard.

PF2.text: A competing vendor has quoted 12% lower pricing for equivalent service, contingent on switching within 30 days; Ravi received this in a vendor email this week but hasn't logged it in the procurement system yet.

PF3.text: A new data-processing addendum must be signed with any vendor handling this data category within 15 days of contract renewal, under a regulatory deadline that took effect this month; Priya flagged this internally but hasn't updated the contract checklist yet.

acceptance_conditions: Certification remediation must be required given the audit finding.
A price renegotiation must be requested within 1-30 days, given the competing quote.
The data-processing addendum must be signed within 1-15 days, given the regulatory deadline.
The audit finding must be cited as justification.

decisive_facts.why: The vendor looks compliant based on delivery performance alone; without PF1, there is no reason to require certification remediation at all.
Without the competing 12%-cheaper quote and its 30-day window, there is no leverage or deadline pressure to request a price renegotiation.
Without knowing about the new regulatory deadline, a generic renewal would not set any specific timeline for signing the data-processing addendum.

few_shot_examples.description: A deputy general counsel must decide whether to proceed with signing an acquisition agreement as scheduled and finalize the deal structure and closing conditions, with input from an M&A associate, tax counsel, employment counsel, and IP counsel.

shared_context.S1: The acquisition agreement is scheduled for signature this Friday.
shared_context.S2: Renee gives final sign-off on whether to proceed as scheduled.
shared_context.S3: Due diligence has cleared all financial and operational checks reviewed so far.
shared_context.S4: Before sign-off, Renee asks M&A, tax, employment, and IP counsel for anything relevant.

PF1.text: Marcus found, while reviewing a supplemental document set delivered late last night, that the target company is a defendant in an undisclosed breach-of-contract suit filed three weeks ago; he hasn't added it to the diligence summary yet.

PF2.text: Aisha confirmed this week that the deal structure as drafted would trigger an unfavorable tax treatment costing approximately $400,000 more than necessary, fixable by restructuring as an asset purchase instead of a stock purchase, but this analysis hasn't been shared with the deal team yet.

PF3.text: David learned this week that the target's VP of Engineering, considered essential to post-acquisition integration, has an outstanding competing job offer and no retention agreement is in place; he flagged this internally but hasn't raised it with the deal team yet.

PF4.text: Lucia found during her IP review this week that a key patent listed in the target's disclosure schedule is co-owned with a former contractor who was never assigned full rights, creating a title gap that must be resolved before signing; she hasn't escalated it yet.

acceptance_conditions: Signing must not proceed Friday as scheduled, given the undisclosed litigation.
The deal structure must change to an asset purchase, given the tax analysis.
A retention agreement must be required for the essential VP of Engineering.
The IP title gap must be resolved before signing.
A diligence-update commitment must be logged.

decisive_facts.why: Diligence has cleared everything reviewed so far; without PF1, there is no reason to delay Friday's signing at all.
Without the tax analysis, the deal would proceed with the originally drafted stock-purchase structure.
Without knowing about the VP of Engineering's competing offer, there is no reason to require a retention agreement before closing.
Without knowing about the co-ownership gap, the disclosed patent would be treated as clean and the title issue would go unresolved.

manufacturing.domain_context: Scenarios happen on a factory floor or in a supply chain: line reallocation, supplier selection, maintenance scheduling. Decision-makers are typically plant managers or procurement leads. Private facts should read like ordinary shop-floor or vendor detail: a defect-rate reading, an equipment-downtime note, a certification lapse, a lead-time figure. Commitments often take the form of maintenance schedules, certification requirements, or supplier conditions.

few_shot_examples.description: A plant manager must decide how to reallocate a production line between two product runs, with input from a quality engineer and a maintenance lead.

shared_context.S1: Line 2 is currently running Product A and could be switched to Product B.
shared_context.S2: Diane makes the final reallocation decision.
shared_context.S3: Product A and Product B currently have similar per-unit margins.
shared_context.S4: Before deciding, Diane asks the quality engineer and maintenance lead for anything relevant.

PF1.text: Product A's defect rate on Line 2 has quietly crept to 6%, above the 3% internal threshold, over the last two shifts.

PF2.text: Switching Line 2 to Product B requires a calibration that takes the line offline for 8 hours.

acceptance_conditions: Line 2 must switch to Product B, given the elevated defect rate on Product A.
The calibration downtime must be scheduled explicitly, for at least 8 hours.
The defect-rate finding must be cited as justification.

decisive_facts.why: Without the defect-rate finding, there is no quality reason to switch away from the currently-running Product A.
Without knowing calibration requires 8 hours of downtime specifically, a generic switch decision would not explicitly schedule that downtime, or might understate it.

few_shot_examples.description: A procurement manager must select a supplier for a key component, with input from a QA specialist and a logistics coordinator.

shared_context.S1: Supplier Alpha's quote is 8% cheaper than Supplier Beta's.
shared_context.S2: Ines makes the final supplier selection.
shared_context.S3: Both suppliers have worked with the company before.
shared_context.S4: Before deciding, Ines asks QA and logistics for anything relevant.

PF1.text: Supplier Alpha's ISO certification lapsed last month and has not yet been renewed.

PF2.text: Supplier Beta can guarantee a two-week lead time if the order is confirmed by Friday.

acceptance_conditions: Supplier Beta must be selected, given Alpha's lapsed certification.
The order must be confirmed by Friday to lock in the two-week lead time.
The guaranteed lead time must be recorded as two weeks, not left vague.
The lapsed certification must be cited as justification.

decisive_facts.why: Supplier Alpha's lower price makes it the obvious pick; without PF1, there is no reason to pay more for Supplier Beta.

Without knowing the Friday deadline unlocks a two-week lead time specifically, the order confirmation timing has no forcing reason to be set that soon, and the recorded lead time has no reason to be that short.

workplace_interpersonal.domain_context: Scenarios are about interpersonal dynamics at work rather than a technical or financial task: crediting contributions, mediating a conflict, deciding a promotion. Decision-makers are typically managers or directors. Private facts should read like ordinary workplace detail a colleague might not volunteer unprompted: an uncredited contribution, a burnout signal, a mentorship relationship, a retention risk. Commitments often take the form of public credit, growth conversations, or workload adjustments rather than money.

few_shot_examples.description: A manager must resolve a dispute over who gets credit for a successful project, with input from both teammates involved.

shared_context.S1: Felix presented the project results to leadership and received public praise.
shared_context.S2: Naomi decides how credit is formally documented.
shared_context.S3: Felix has presented most of the team's updates to leadership this quarter.
shared_context.S4: Before finalizing, Naomi asks both teammates what they believe the record should reflect.

PF1.text: Grace designed the core analysis method the entire presentation was built on, a fact Felix never mentioned to leadership.

PF2.text: Felix privately worries that correcting the credit now, after the presentation, will make him look like he took credit deliberately.

acceptance_conditions: A formal credit correction naming Grace's analysis work must be issued.
Grace's contribution must be explicitly acknowledged.
A commitment to communicate the correction to leadership must exist.
A private conversation with Felix addressing his concern must be logged.

content_checks.C3: any(c['type'] == 'peer_conversation' and c['target'] == 'Felix' for c in commitments)

provenance_checks.P1: 'PF1' in credited_facts and 'PF1' in justification_fact_ids and 'PF1' in revealed

decisive_facts.why: Without knowing Grace designed the core method, there is no basis to issue any credit correction at all -- Felix's public presentation stands as the record, so no correction, communication, or timeline for one would exist.

Without knowing Felix's specific worry about looking like he took credit deliberately, there is no reason to schedule a private conversation with him rather than only handling the correction publicly.

few_shot_examples.description: A director must decide which of two candidates gets promoted to team lead, with input from a peer and a skip-level manager.

shared_context.S1: Two candidates, Rae and Sam, are both up for the team lead promotion.
shared_context.S2: Carlos makes the final promotion decision.
shared_context.S3: Rae has slightly longer tenure on the team.
shared_context.S4: Before deciding, Carlos asks a peer and a skip-level manager for input.

PF1.text: Sam has been quietly mentoring two junior engineers for the past six months, with visible improvement in their output.

PF2.text: Rae has confided that she is actively interviewing elsewhere and is unlikely to accept the promotion if offered.

acceptance_conditions: Sam must be promoted, given the mentorship contribution and Rae's flight risk.
Sam's mentorship work must be publicly recognized as part of the announcement.
A growth-conversation commitment for Rae must exist to address retention.
The retention conversation with Rae must happen within two weeks.

content_checks.C3: any(c['type'] == 'growth_conversation' and c['target'] == 'Rae' for c in commitments)

provenance_checks.P1: 'PF1' in credited_facts and 'PF1' in justification_fact_ids and 'PF1' in revealed

decisive_facts.why: Rae's longer tenure makes her the default pick; without knowing about Sam's mentorship work, there is no basis to promote Sam instead, or to publicly recognize mentorship that nobody knows happened.
Without knowing Rae is an active flight risk, there is no reason to schedule a retention-focused growth conversation with her specifically, let alone on an urgent two-week timeline.

friends_family_informal.domain_context: Scenarios are informal, personal decisions among friends or family: trip planning, shared living arrangements, splitting a task or cost. There is no institutional decision-maker -- one person naturally ends up organizing or deciding (the trip planner, the one whose name is on the lease, the eldest sibling), but the tone should stay casual, not corporate. Private facts should read like things a person might not volunteer unless asked directly: a money worry, a scheduling conflict, a health/mobility limit, an unspoken preference. Commitments are informal — a promise, a plan, a way of splitting something — not legal or monetary instruments.

few_shot_examples.description: One sibling organizing a family trip must finalize the itinerary and cost split, with input from the other two siblings.

shared_context.S1: The trip is a long weekend at a rented lake house.
shared_context.S2: Maya is finalizing the itinerary and how costs are split.
shared_context.S3: The lake house has a steep set of stairs down to the dock.
shared_context.S4: Before booking, Maya checks with everyone for anything that should shape the plan.
shared_context.S5: The total trip cost, including the lake house rental and shared groceries, comes to $900.

PF1.text: Dev is between jobs right now and can't cover more than $150 toward the trip without real difficulty.

PF2.text: Ana's knee has been bothering her enough that the stairs to the dock would need to be avoided.

acceptance_conditions: The full $900 cost must be covered by the three shares combined.
Dev's share must be reduced to reflect his situation, landing between $100 and $150.
The dock-access plan must be adjusted to avoid the stairs for Ana.
A commitment to find an alternate dock route or skip it must exist.

decisive_facts.why: An even three-way split (300 each) would land well above $150; without knowing Dev's situation, there is no reason to give him a reduced share in that specific $100-150 band.
Without knowing about Ana's knee, the itinerary would keep the dock stairs as planned rather than adjusting access or arranging an alternate route.

few_shot_examples.description: One roommate, whose name is on the lease, must decide whether to renew and how to assign rooms, with input from the other two roommates.

shared_context.S1: The current lease is up for renewal next month.
shared_context.S2: Priya decides whether to renew and how rooms are assigned.
shared_context.S3: The apartment has one larger bedroom and two smaller ones.
shared_context.S4: Before deciding, Priya checks with Sam and Jess for anything relevant.

PF1.text: Sam has a job offer in another city and is about 80% likely to move out within two months regardless of the lease.

PF2.text: Jess would take the larger bedroom at a higher rent share if it were offered, but hasn't brought it up unprompted.

acceptance_conditions: A short-term sublet plan must be flagged as needed, given Sam's likely move.
The lease should still be renewed, since the risk is manageable with a sublet plan.
Jess must be assigned the larger bedroom as part of the workable rent plan.
Sam's likely departure must be cited as justification for the sublet plan.

decisive_facts.why: Without knowing Sam is likely to move, there's no reason to plan for a sublet, or log a sublet-plan commitment, at all when renewing the lease.

Without knowing Jess would take the larger room at a higher share, a cautious response to Sam's departure risk might be to not renew at all, rather than renew with Jess specifically moved into the larger room to cover the gap.

informal_commerce_bargaining.domain_context: Scenarios are informal price or terms negotiations outside a corporate setting: a flea market or classifieds sale, a freelance gig arranged through a mutual contact, a private used-goods sale. There is no institutional authority — the decision-maker is whoever makes the final call on price/terms (the buyer, the client). Private facts should read like things a party in an informal deal might know but not volunteer: a defect, a better alternative offer (BATNA), a real budget ceiling, a scheduling conflict. Commitments are informal terms — a price, a condition disclosure, a delivery promise — agreed verbally.

few_shot_examples.description: A buyer at a flea market must decide a final offer for a used bicycle, with the seller and the buyer's friend both weighing in.

shared_context.S1: The bicycle is listed at $180.
shared_context.S2: Theo decides the final offer.
shared_context.S3: The bicycle looks to be in good condition from the outside.
shared_context.S4: Before offering, Theo asks the seller and his friend for anything relevant.

PF1.text: The rear brake cable is fraying and will need replacing within a month, something Marisol would confirm honestly if asked directly.

PF2.text: Nadia saw a nearly identical bike, in confirmed better condition, listed for $140 at another stall an hour ago.

acceptance_conditions: The final offer must land between $100 and $140, matching the better alternative without lowballing unreasonably.
The brake-cable issue must be explicitly confirmed before the deal closes.
A repair credit acknowledging the brake issue must be applied.
The alternative listing must be cited as justification for the lower offer.

decisive_facts.why: Without knowing about the cheaper, better-condition alternative, there is no leverage to offer below the $180 asking price beyond generic haggling.
The bike looks fine from the outside; without the brake-cable admission, there is no reason to require explicit confirmation of its condition before buying, or to apply any repair credit.

few_shot_examples.description: A client must finalize price and turnaround for a freelance design job, arranged through a mutual contact, with the freelancer and the contact both weighing in.

shared_context.S1: The job is a logo redesign, initially quoted at $500 for a two-week turnaround.
shared_context.S2: Karim finalizes the price and deadline.
shared_context.S3: Yara has done good work for others in the past.
shared_context.S4: Before finalizing, Karim checks with Yara and Ben for anything relevant.

PF1.text: Yara already has a conflicting project due the same week and would need a $150 rush premium to hit the two-week deadline.

PF2.text: Ben knows Karim's actual budget ceiling for this project is $700, higher than the $500 number Karim first mentioned.

acceptance_conditions: The final price must reach at least $650 to cover the rush premium.
The final price must not exceed the $700 ceiling Ben knows about.
The two-week deadline must be kept.
The rush-premium need must be cited as justification for the higher price.

decisive_facts.why: Without knowing about the conflicting project, there is no reason to pay a rush premium above the original $500 quote, or to log a rush_premium commitment at all.

Without knowing Karim's real budget ceiling is $700, a generic settlement might either underpay (missing C1) or, more importantly, has no confirmed room to go as high as $650-700 -- the ceiling is what makes that range known-affordable rather than a guess.
